title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop affects verifier-detected safety violations for LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared LLM proposal validated by a deterministic netops verifier and subjected to up to one automated repair iteration if the verifier flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). The preregistered exact McNemar two-sided test was implemented as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01) with two-sided p computed as 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} for X ∼ Binomial(n, 0.5) (truncated at 1.0); for the observed discordant counts (n = 1, n10 = 1) the archived two-sided p = 1.00 under that convention. Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; measured marginal verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though the verifier corrected at least one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, multi-step change planning, and automated repairs. System reports and surveys emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding engineering: deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback mechanisms [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A widely proposed operational pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): an LLM produces a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks formalized properties, and automated or human-in-the-loop repairs are applied when violations are detected. Practitioners must know: when an LLM already produces high-quality candidates, how much incremental safety does a verifier plus a modest automated repair budget provide on a verifier-scoped pass/fail metric? We answer this narrowly and operationally by preregistering and executing a paired experiment that isolates verifier+repair impact while holding the LLM’s initial proposal identical across arms.
sections.related_work: Two literatures motivate this study. First, deterministic and formal network-configuration verification (header-space analysis, route-model checkers, Batfish-style analyzers) provide machine-checkable properties (reachability, isolation, update atomicity) and are standard references for automated verification in NetOps [Beckett et al., 2017]. Second, recent agentic NetOps/AIOps systems integrate LLMs for intent parsing and configuration generation while advocating guardrails (verifiers, sandboxes, rollbacks) to reduce operational risk (e.g., INTA, Confucius, and other agentic frameworks) [Wei et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair (or generate–critic) patterns appear across structured-generation domains and have been proposed to reduce incorrect or unsafe LLM outputs [PoeTone; INTA]. Failure-mode studies of LLM automation document hallucination, overconfidence, and integration errors that motivate verifier-based mitigations [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. What is less common—especially in the supplied evidence set—is a controlled, preregistered ablation that quantifies the marginal verifier effect while keeping the model’s initial output identical; our work fills that narrow empirical gap.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and hypothesis. We preregistered study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026 and froze: the research question, inclusion/exclusion rules, deterministic task seeds, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule. Confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired per-task). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations. The preregistration and artifacts are archived (preregistration SHA-256 recorded in the execution manifest). Task corpus and stratification. A deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks was created with deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 using preregistered seeds and constrained to verifier-modeled features ({admin, mtu, vlan}). The realized stratified sample matched the preregistered allocation: VLAN-change = 167 tasks, ACL-change = 167 tasks, static-route-change = 166 tasks (sum = 500). Generation semantics and experimental control. To isolate verifier marginal effect we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false). For each task the pipeline produced one shared LLM proposal that served as the baseline output and was also validated by the guarded arm. The guarded path invoked an automated single-repair call only if the deterministic verifier flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on that shared candidate. This design prevents conflation with verifier-guided regeneration and isolates verification+repair applied to the same initial proposal. Models and verifier. Requested LLM = gpt-5-mini called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (provider recorded as openai_responses); model parameters and execution settings are archived in execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini, max_output_tokens = 2000, single-attempt generation). The deterministic verifier used for gating and scoring was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator spec and violation→severity mapping archived). Repair budget. The guarded arm permitted at most one automated repair iteration per preregistration. Primary statistical test. The preregistered confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. The archived implementation forms n = n10 + n01 (discordant pairs) and computes an exact two-sided p via an exact Binomial(n, 0.5) on n10 with two-sided p = 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} (truncated at 1.0). The analysis artifacts and implementation details are archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Bootstrap CI. We computed paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the absolute difference with B = 10,000 resamples and bootstrap_seed = 1729; resampling unit = task/pair with pairing preserved. Missingness and stopping. The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two automated retries for transient provider errors. The run stopped after processing preregistered confirmatory pairs or when adapter model-call budget was reached. Execution-accounting fields (execution manifest) record model_calls_used and repair-stage calls.
sections.results: Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair-stage calls observed = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts are: baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). The paired contingency counts (guarded × baseline) are: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. Exact McNemar two-sided p-value and CI. Using the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention yields two-sided p = 1.00 for the observed discordant counts (n = 1, n10 = 1). The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Repair activity and provenance of discordant pair. Observed repair-stage provider calls = 1. That single repair call produced the sole discordant outcome (n10 = 1): the guarded arm converted one baseline-detected violation into a verified pass. The evidence bundle archives full per-task validator diagnostics and repair traces. The deterministic artifact storing per-task outcomes is execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA-256: e7c1fc4d8932389dc3e4c651cf6db08a84ba3a1cd4893b9d7d985618929ff945); to locate the single discordant episode deterministically filter that file for entries with baseline scoring indicating a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) and guarded scoring indicating a pass (guarded pass == 1). The file contains exactly one such entry (the run-level reconciliation artifacts confirm this). Observed stratification diagnostics. The realized per-cluster counts are explicitly recorded in the archived task_manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and equal the preregistered allocation: VLAN-change = 167, ACL-change = 167, static-route-change = 166. No confirmatory exclusions or contamination flags occurred (analysis/missingness_summary.csv and analysis/contamination_summary.csv show zeros). Power divergence and ceiling effect. The preregistration targeted N = 500 based on an anticipated baseline error prevalence near 0.30; the observed baseline failure prevalence (1/500) created a strong ceiling effect that reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements. As a consequence secondary per-violation-class analyses are uninformative due to near-zero counts. All analysis artifacts (paired contingency table, missingness summary, and deterministic reconciliation) are archived and referenced above.
sections.discussion: Operational interpretation. Under the constrained experimental regime—single requested model (gpt-5-mini), shared_initial_candidate semantics, deterministic verifier coverage limited to {admin, mtu, vlan}, and at most one automated repair—the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals and the marginal measured pass-rate benefit of adding the verifier was small (0.002). This is a conditional result: when baseline proposal quality is very high on the verifier-modeled properties, modest verifier+repair budgets may yield negligible measurable gains on a composite pass/fail metric, even though verifiers can still correct rare concrete failures (one such correction was observed here). Design-choice implications. The shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate the verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals; this is operationally relevant when deployment semantics favor repairing a single human-reviewed proposal instead of regenerating new candidates. We do not evaluate verifier-guided regeneration, multiple repair iterations, or cost-weighted loss functions; those alternatives could yield larger effect sizes and require separate preregistered evaluation. Threats to validity. Internal validity is supported by preregistration, deterministic seeds, and automated replacement rules; no manual adjudication occurred. Construct validity is limited by verifier coverage: success==no preregistered high/medium-severity violations is defined relative to the verifier’s modeled property set (archived in the validator-spec artifacts). External validity is limited by single-model testing, synthetic corpus, and restricted feature scope—results do not generalize beyond the verifier’s modeled semantics or to heterogeneous vendor CLIs. Statistical nuance. The archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the executor’s exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the empirical discordant counts (n = 1). Small-sample exact p-values under this convention are non-intuitive; here p = 1.00 indicates the observed discordant pattern is not improbable under the null when n is so small. The paired-bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.006] provides complementary uncertainty quantification for the absolute difference. Operational recommendations. (1) Measure baseline proposal error prevalence on representative operational data before committing expensive repair budgets: when baseline error is extremely low on verifier-scoped properties, marginal pass-rate gains per unit cost may be small. (2) Align verifier property coverage with operator-critical constraints and expand the verifier where production-critical properties are outside current coverage. (3) Choose generation semantics that match deployment priorities: shared-initial semantics conserve model calls and preserve the original candidate, while regeneration-based guarded workflows may improve pass probability at higher model-call cost.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), giving an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the run’s exact-binomial convention). This conditional measurement illustrates a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is very high for verifier-modeled properties and verifier coverage is limited, the measurable marginal pass-rate benefit of a modest verifier+repair budget can be negligible on a composite pass/fail metric, though the verifier can still correct rare concrete failures. Practitioners should quantify baseline error prevalence, align verifier coverage with operator priorities, and select generation/repair semantics appropriate for their cost and safety trade-offs. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection (see execution/* and analysis/* artifact paths and SHA-256s referenced in the Disclosure Statement).

limitations: Synthetic deterministic task corpus constrained to features modeled by the deterministic validator; task payloads limited to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model or cross-validator generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA-256: e7c1fc4d8932389dc3e4c651cf6db08a84ba3a1cd4893b9d7d985618929ff945). To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces.
